title: Most harm we do ourselves
hook: he argues most suffering comes from what people do to themselves and each other

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: providence follows attention. The leaf, the spider, and the palace where a wandering mind drifts out. What did you give your whole attention to? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

A writer once argued that the world holds more evil than good. Count up the pain, the sickness, the grief, he said, and the scale tips the wrong way. Maimonides read that argument and answered it in the Guide. He didn't deny that suffering is real. He did something more uncomfortable. He sorted it, kind by kind, and asked where it actually comes from. And when the sorting was done, the biggest pile wasn't the one blamed on God or on nature. Today's word is the label on that pile.
screen: `MORE EVIL THAN GOOD?` → `SORT THE SUFFERING.` → `WHICH PILE IS BIGGEST?`

segments.voice: Most harm we do ourselves. It comes from the twelfth chapter of the third part of the Guide. Turn it four ways. First, the harm of having a body. Bodies come into being and wear out. Illness, injury, the blows of nature. This kind is real, Maimonides says, but compared with the others, it is less frequent. Second, the harm people do to each other. Tyranny, violence, war. This kind is more common than the first, he says. But it's still not the largest. Third, the harm people do to themselves. And this, he says, is the most frequent of all. Too much eating, too much drinking, appetites without limits, chasing more than anyone needs. A person wrecks their health, their peace, their relationships, and then complains about the world. Some readers find in his discussion that the hunger for luxuries also turns people against each other, so the third kind feeds the second. He quotes Ecclesiastes: "God made man upright; but they have sought out many inventions." Fourth, why the writer got it wrong. A person who thinks the whole universe exists for them, Maimonides says, judges everything by their own small hurts, and so concludes the world is mostly bad. But step back, and much of what we suffer turns out to be within reach of human choice. This is not a teaching that blames people for their illnesses or their grief. Maimonides keeps the first kind in the list. It's a teaching that hands back some power: the largest pile is the one people can begin to shrink.
screen: `THE BODY WEARS OUT.` · `WHAT PEOPLE DO TO EACH OTHER.` · `WHAT PEOPLE DO TO THEMSELVES.` · `THE WORLD IS NOT ABOUT ME.` · then, large: `MOST HARM WE DO OURSELVES.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe at an easy pace. Think back over the past week. Bring up one thing that hurt or went wrong. Then sort it, gently, the way Maimonides would. Was it the body, or nature, simply happening? Was it something another person did? Or was some part of it mine: a habit, an excess, a word I chose? Don't punish yourself. Just find the part, however small, that's yours. Then decide on one step to take responsibility for it. Cutting back one excess. Changing one habit. Saying one thing differently next time. The bell holds the time.

Most harm we do ourselves. Maimonides' teaching that of the three kinds of suffering, the most frequent is what people bring on themselves, and much of the rest is what they do to each other. Today's word.
screen: `MOST HARM WE DO OURSELVES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: most harm we do. Today, take the one step you chose, the excess cut back or the habit changed, even for one day. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Jewish teaching on repentance asks a person to examine their own part in what went wrong, and some study Maimonides' account of the three kinds of evil in Guide 3:12 alongside his Laws of Repentance.

fork.setup: you're Maimonides. a writer argues the world holds more evil than good. how do you answer?
options: agree, and say nothing can be done.
sort suffering by kind, and show most comes from people.
fork.reveal: he sorts it into three kinds and finds the largest is what people do to themselves. the writer, he says, judged the universe by his own hurts.

trapdoor: what you thought: most suffering comes from God, or from bad luck.
what it means: Maimonides finds that the harm people do to themselves is the most frequent, and harm to each other comes next.
what a scholar hears: Guide 3:12's three kinds of evil, his reply to a writer who said evil outweighs good, and Ecclesiastes 7:29.

notes: Guide 3:12 paraphrased: three kinds of evil (from being material/natural; people to each other; people to themselves), the third the most frequent, the first the least; his reply to al-Razi (unnamed here as 'a writer') who held evils outnumber goods.
